set.rappel_count_note: Four rappels on a single 60 m rope used doubled, each under 30 m, reversing the four pitches back to Pineapple Pass - this is what almost every party does and how the stations are spaced. One 60 m rappel in the sequence comes up just short of the next tree, leaving a short unroped downscramble, which an added pitch-3 anchor now avoids. A separate, partly hidden bolted line beside pitches 1 and 2 exists so that ascending and descending parties are not in the same place; it is a different set of anchors, not a variation. Below Pineapple Pass the east gully holds two more bolted chain stations for two further rappels on a 60 m - optional, and many parties scramble out instead; there is meaningful rockfall hazard in that gully. Do not scramble directly up to Pineapple Pass on the way in: that ground is the rappel route.

review.single_rope: Four rappels on a single 60 m rope, each about 30 m or less, back to Pineapple Pass; existing table already fits one rope (all stations 30 m).

set.rappels: About 4-5 rappels down the ridge on a single rope, from existing fixed slings; a single 60 m rope works and a 70 m rope is more comfortable
set.rappel_count_note: Parties have made about four or five rappels down the ridge, from the summit block onward, using existing slings. A single 60 m rope is enough for them, and a 70 m rope is recommended for reaching the stations comfortably. Exact station spacing and lengths are not recorded, so no station table is given.
set.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the ridge itself on a single rope — most parties use a 70m rope to reach the stations comfortably, and a single 60m rope also works. Existing fixed rap slings have been reported along the route.

set.rappel_count_note: The published descent is five rappels: from the top of pitch 8 to the top of pitch 7, then to the anchor next to the Duck, then three down the gully to the base. Rappel lengths are not published and the stations are not documented as reachable on one 60 m rope. Treat a single-rope descent as unconfirmed: be ready to downclimb or build an intermediate anchor, and check each station before pulling the rope.

set.rappel_count_note: Parties describe two to three rappels through the chimney-and-ramp section, on a single 60 m rope; the count varies with how much is downclimbed. The first anchor is usually old fixed tat; expect to build natural anchors for the rest. Lengths are not published.
set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line off the North Peak summit. Parties describe two to three rappels getting back down through the 4th/low-5th-class chimney-and-ramp section to easier 3rd-class ground above the glacier — plan on a single 60m rope. The first rappel station is commonly an old fixed sling/tat anchor left by previous parties, but it should not be trusted blindly — inspect it or back it up, and be prepared to build natural gear anchors (cams/nuts on horns or cracks) for the remaining stations since fixed gear is inconsistent year to year. After the rappels, downclimb/scramble the remaining 3rd-class terrain back to the col, reverse the ~1,000 ft descent to the glacier, re-cross the Queest-Alb Glacier (watch the moat and any crevasses), climb back up to Tin Can Gap, and reverse Trail #641 through Goat Flats and Saddle Lake to the trailhead. Rockfall in the chimney/gully and a icy glacier moat are the main descent-specific hazards; a mid-to-late-season descent in soft/rotten snow on the glacier headwall can also be tricky.
